title: Bad News Comes From You First
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This short Admired Leadership piece sets out a single operating rule for anyone who reports to a leader: when something goes wrong, the leader must hear it from you before hearing it from anyone else. The argument frames the delivery of bad news as a test of credibility, measured by the confidence and speed with which it is brought forward. It explains the leader's side of the equation, noting that leaders need early warning to field questions, rally support and release resources. When the news arrives secondhand, the piece argues, trust breaks and the leader begins to wonder what else is being withheld and whether the subordinate is competent to handle the problem. It insists on direct, personal contact rather than voicemail, text or email, and offers the practical example of leaving an urgent message before boarding a plane. The piece closes with a memorable contrast: good news can take the scenic route, but bad news requires the express lane.
points: Delivering bad news is recast as a credibility test, judged by the confidence and alacrity with which a subordinate brings it forward rather than by the news itself.
When a leader learns of a problem from another source, the damage extends beyond the incident: they begin to question what else is not being disclosed.
Written channels such as voicemail, text and email are ruled out for bad news; credible leaders reach their own leader directly and immediately.
Even when direct contact is impossible, signalling urgency in advance (such as a message left before a flight) shows the leader you were trying to tell them first.
The closing rule, that bad news never improves with age and must come from you first, gives the reader a portable standard for managing up.
quotes: Leaders hate to be surprised by bad news. The good ones would rather hear about what occurred immediately so they can prepare for whatever questions they might receive.
The bad news must come from you first before others beat you to it. Your credibility is being tested. It’s measured by the level of confidence and alacrity you bring in delivering the bad news.

Unless your leader hears from you directly, they question what else you might not be telling them. Their suspicions concern them for a good reason. People who can be trusted to solve the problem are never shy about communicating the problem.
Trust is broken when leaders learn from other sources what has occurred. By the time you offer the bad news, they are already in a state of dismay.
Voicemails, texts, or emails don’t cut it. For bad news, credible leaders get to their leader directly and as quickly as possible.
When they hear the news before you land, they know you were trying to tell them directly. This helps to allay their deepest fears — that you lack the mettle to deliver the bad news.
The rule to remember is that bad news always comes from you first. Good leaders never forget that. Let good news take the scenic route.
